questions.q: What is the standard SI unit used to measure the voltage supplied by an electric cell or a battery?
questions.a: The correct unit is the Volt (V). A wrong answer usually confuses voltage with electric current (measured in Amperes) or electrical resistance (measured in Ohms), showing a failure to link physical quantities to their correct measuring units.

questions.q: Why must the positive terminal of one electric cell be connected to the negative terminal of the next cell when forming a battery, rather than connecting positive to positive?
questions.a: Connecting positive to negative ensures that the electrical pushes of the individual cells add up to increase the total voltage. If positive is connected to positive, their opposing voltages will cancel each other out, resulting in zero net voltage for the circuit. A wrong answer shows a lack of understanding of polarity and how potentials combine in series.

questions.q: If a single dry cell has a voltage of 1.5 V, what will be the total voltage of a battery made by connecting 3 such identical cells in a proper series combination?
questions.a:
The correct answer is 4.5 V. 
Steps: 
1. Identify the voltage of one cell: $V_1 = 1.5\text{ V}$.
2. Identify the number of cells connected in series: $n = 3$.
3. Apply the series voltage addition rule: $\text{Total Voltage} = V_1 \times n$.
4. Compute: $1.5\text{ V} \times 3 = 4.5\text{ V}$.
A wrong answer, such as 1.5 V or multiplying incorrectly, reveals that the student does not understand how voltages accumulate in a series cell combination.

questions.q: A torchlight requires 3.0 V to glow brightly, but you only have cells that provide 1.5 V each. How many cells must you use, and how must they be arranged to make the torchlight work?
questions.a: You must use 2 cells connected in series, where the positive terminal of the first cell touches the negative terminal of the second cell. A wrong answer indicates confusion about how multiple cells are combined to meet the required operating voltage of an electrical appliance.

questions.q: Suppose a student connects four 1.5 V cells in a battery holder, but accidentally inserts one cell facing backward (positive touching positive). What will be the effective total voltage of this 4-cell battery pack?
questions.a:
The effective total voltage will be 3.0 V. 
Reasoning: Three cells pointing in the correct direction give $3 \times 1.5\text{ V} = 4.5\text{ V}$, but the one backward cell subtracts $1.5\text{ V}$, leaving $4.5\text{ V} - 1.5\text{ V} = 3.0\text{ V}$. A wrong answer shows that the student fails to account for opposing polarities cancelling out individual cell potentials.

questions.q: Give the correct order of connections for wiring three lemon cells so their voltages add up to light an LED.
questions.a: The series chain runs: (1) Place one copper and one zinc strip in each lemon (2) Join the copper strip of the first lemon to the zinc strip of the second (3) Join the copper of the second to the zinc of the third (4) Connect the two free ends, one copper and one zinc, to the LED terminals with correct polarity. A wrong answer that pairs like metals together shows the student does not understand that a battery adds cell voltages only when every cell pushes current in the same direction along the chain.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: A battery is a ______ of two or more electric cells connected together to provide a higher total voltage and sustained electric current to a circuit.
Fill in the blank: When you look inside a TV remote control or a large wall clock, you notice that ______ cylindrical electric cells are placed end-to-end rather than just a single cell.
What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: Can correctly connect two or more electric cells in series (positive terminal of one connected to the negative terminal of the next) to light up a bulb requiring higher voltage, and can calculate the total voltage by summing individual cell voltages.
